chapter_theme: The hero worships the renounced women and a queen of the court gives up pleasure for austerity; the ministers, afraid he will follow, fill a pool for a water-battle in which the women are beaten by the king, and the chapter closes in the pleasures of the couch, the last enjoyment before his own turning away.

cast.role: the hero, here the king, unnamed in these verses
Civakan's wife, who sprays and fights on in the water-war
the ministers who build the pool to keep the king from renouncing
the king's honoured lady who gives up pleasure for austerity
the daughter of the mountain king who takes the enemy's part in the game
the women of the court who play and lose the water-war
the slender woman who takes the king's garland and loses her silk
the saffron-vined women who ride in procession to the palace
the mothers-in-law who send the women off

2649.reading: Having praised the feet of the women who renounced as flowers resting on his head, the garlanded hero goes and enters the great fragrant temple.
2649.nuance: The nun-like figure behind கந்தி and the antecedent of the pronouns are not given in the verse.
2649.event: The hero worships the renounced women's feet and enters the temple.

2650.reading: Sent off by the mothers-in-law, the saffron-vined women ride a gem-canopied palanquin guarded by spearmen and enter the flag-lined palace.
2650.nuance: Whether these are the women of the preceding verse or the hero's wives cannot be fixed from the verse.
2650.event: The women, dismissed by their mothers-in-law, go in procession to the palace.

2651.reading: The king's honoured lady, like a doll of pure gem, gives up pleasure that is like a rain-bubble, puts away desire and takes up the austerity of her line, living like a goddess.
2651.nuance: The poem shows renunciation by a woman of the court before the hero turns to it himself, and gives the bubble image as the reason.
2651.event: The king's lady gives up enjoyment and takes to austerity.

claims.claim: worldly pleasure is as short-lived as a rain-bubble and is to be given up with desire

2652.reading: The poet of the sea-shore, with its swans and lilies, says he will now tell what befell the umbrella-king.
2652.nuance: A poet's turn to a new matter, in the narrator's own voice.

2653.reading: Fearing that the king will turn towards renunciation, the ministers work to keep him in the pleasure of the women and fill a water-tank with scented water.
2653.nuance: The ministers' fear (துறவின்பாற் படர்தல் அஞ்சி) states the cause of the whole water-sport: it is a device against his leaving.
2653.event: The ministers, fearing his turn to renunciation, prepare a pleasure-pond to hold the king.

2654.reading: The ministers fill the tank with floats, garlands, sandal paste, gem syringes and powders for the women and the king, and ask the lord to come and see it.
2654.event: The ministers equip the pool and invite the king to come and see it.

2655.reading: The women are drawn into two armies, with the mountain king's daughter taking the enemy general's part and the rest the king's host, and they open a water-war with garlands, powder and syringes.
2655.nuance: கட்டியங்காரன் here is a role in the game, not the usurping minister of the story; the mountain-king's daughter is not named.
2655.event: The women divide into the king's army and the mock enemy and begin the water-battle.

2656.reading: The women strike with flower garlands that scatter bees, hurl lotus chains of bells like discs and let garlands fall like arrows, so that the tangle of garlands is their weapon.
2656.event: The women fight with flower garlands used as arms.

2657.reading: Gandharvadattai takes up a syringe of red water and sends a thousand streams, and the women, unable to bear it, plunge like lightning into a cloud, with their eyes reddened by the cold water.
2657.event: Gandharvadattai sprays the women, who dive into the water.

2658.reading: The women climb the pool's pavilion and leap in like peacocks coming down from the sky, and rise from the clear water like lakshmis or like a moon newly risen on the dewy sea.
2658.event: The women leap from the pavilion into the pool.

2659.reading: Struck with garlands the women sag and falter, beg with powder and sandal falling, bend to the thrown garlands and melt like butter.
2659.event: The women, struck with garlands, melt and plead for mercy.

2660.reading: The women with their hair in one hand and their silk in the other, unable to watch where they step, run to the king for refuge, and he, seeing their distress, takes up a golden syringe and pours like a rain-cloud.
2660.nuance: The king's anger is playful: காய்ந்து is the word for it, set against a pour compared to rain.
2660.event: The women flee to the king, who answers with his own syringe.

2661.reading: The king looses streams, the women let their garlands and powder and perfumed cloths fall, and the army of the love-god, defeated in the war, is routed.
2661.nuance: The battle names the love-god's army as the women's, and it is the women who lose; Kama's army is beaten by the king in play.
2661.event: The king's streams win; the women's garlands and cloth fall and the love-god's army is routed.

2662.reading: The beaten women turn into swans among lotuses, peacocks hiding in their hair, lotuses laying faces on his, and give up their girdles and earrings and bow to touch his feet.
2662.event: The defeated women submit, giving girdles and earrings and touching his feet.

2663.reading: The women who have lost their garlands and silk stand wrapped only in a white foam, their lightning-like bodies shaking, looking to the king.
2663.nuance: The first two lines compare the women's eyes and the snatching of garlands in a way the verse does not make clear.
2663.event: The women, stripped of garlands and silk by the sport, stand looking at the king.

2664.reading: Her ranks broken, Gandharvadattai binds on a stream of sandal and, running with nine jets, sprays red powder over the king's wide chest and begins to twist its force against him.
2664.nuance: Gandharvadattai is named in 2657 and again here, the one wife who stays to fight on.
2664.event: Gandharvadattai, her side broken, turns a nine-jet stream of red powder on the king's chest.

2665.reading: A slender woman with a hand-weapon stands before the king and takes his garland; he, undone, stands helpless as she tries to bind and throw the other woman by force.
2665.nuance: The pronouns of the last two lines are hard to fix; I read the king as the one who stands helpless.
2665.event: A woman disarms the king of his garland and the game turns on him.

2666.reading: The sandal and powder are carried off by the water, and the slender woman's silk is lost and her gold girdle lies silent; looking at the king she asks what has fallen, and shy, embraces him like the sun joined with lightning.
2666.event: A woman loses her silk to the water and, ashamed, embraces the king.

2667.reading: After the sport the women steam their bodies with agil smoke, dry their fragrant hair, put on fine silk and set anicham garlands in their tresses.
2667.event: The women dry and dress themselves after the water-sport.

2668.reading: They say the women, with bright garlands, enjoyed the grace of the man with mountain-like shoulders whose body the water had heated.
2668.nuance: The metre changes here; the opening lines are hard to read exactly and the verse is closed with என்பவே, 'they say'.
2668.event: The women enjoy the king's company after the water-sport.

2669.reading: In the heat of summer the king lies on a couch cooled by sandal paste and moon-rays, staying on the breasts of the woman who lies with him.
2669.event: The king rests with a woman on a sandal-cooled couch.

2670.reading: Her gem ornaments seem to weep pearls, her brow like a vine bends in worship and the flowers of her hair sink as if she were tired with the whole body's pleasure.
2670.event: A woman gives her whole body to pleasure with the king.

2671.reading: The women, like coral boughs of the wishing-tree, know writing, song and dance, and the king, in their company, is the very love-god of the five-arrow love-god.
2671.nuance: The compliment makes the king the love-god of the love-god, setting him above the god he has just defeated in the water-war of 2661.

2672.reading: Frightened by the thunder of the clouds, the women with their hair like a rain-cloud's shadow embrace the king and gain the beauty of boughs clinging to a tree.
2672.event: The women, frightened by thunder, cling to the king.

2673.reading: The women descend to the low agil-scented couch, their sandal paste wiped off, their breasts bruised by garlands, and their girdles and anklets sounding as they fall apart.
2673.event: The women lie with the king on the low couch, their paste and girdles undone.

links.note: The queen puts away pleasure for austerity; Naladiyar 53 says the best of people consider slowly and give up home, youth and beauty without delay.
links.teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's counsel taken by a woman at the court while her husband is still held by pleasure, which makes giving up one's own household look like a path that is left open and not forced.

gains.a: The queen's austerity, narrated in one verse, gets a stated reason: the things she gives up are the short-lived goods of the quatrain.
gains.b: The quatrain's counsel of quick renunciation meets a case from a royal house, where the one who gives up is a wife and not the head of the family.

links.note: In 1946 the breasts of the sandal-painted women turn even those who think of release back; in 2651 a woman of the court puts pleasure down and goes to austerity.
links.teaches: The poem keeps both outcomes in front of the reader: the same world of women that can undo a renouncer can also be left by one of its own members.

links.note: The king wins the love-god's war in play, with garlands and streams; Naladiyar 17 says youth drops like fruit and the woman desired for her spear-like eyes will walk with a staff.
links.teaches: The epic's delight at its brightest is the thing the quatrain tells the hearer not to desire, so the water-sport is set to be read against the old age it will bring.

gains.a: The verse's triumph over the love-god gains a time limit: the women who yield are those who will one day lean on staffs.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning gains a concrete scene of the pleasure it warns against, with garlands, powder and a king at play.

links.note: The women dress, steam and garland themselves after the play; Naladiyar 16 likens the joy of youth to a lamb nibbling at the garland held out before the slaughter.
links.teaches: The same garland that is the sign of pleasure in the Cintamani is the bait of the sacrifice in the quatrain, and the reader sees both uses of one object.

gains.a: The garland-wearing at the end of the sport gains a darker reading, in which the adornment is what precedes the loss.
gains.b: The quatrain's lamb and garland gain a courtly setting where the garland is a gift of love and not a rite.

links.note: The couch scene rubs off the sandal and tears at the garlands; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing the body they decorate.
links.teaches: Both pass through sandal, garland and body, one to delight in them and one to say the body is the cart that vultures will tear at.

gains.a: The sandal rubbed off the women's breasts gains the quatrain's view of what lies under it, the body that decays.
gains.b: The quatrain's sandal and garlands gain a scene in which they are being worn and spoiled in the way that it mocks.

links.note: In 67 women plunge into the country pools and their girdle strings break and scatter; in 2662 the defeated women in the king's pool give up their girdles and earrings to him.
links.teaches: The scattering of gold that the landscape verse shows as nature's wealth is shown here as a gift laid at the king's feet, which changes whose ornament it is.

links.note: In 1996 Civakan praises Vimalai's breasts as enough to make the released fall; in 2671 the king, with women skilled in writing, song and dance, is called the love-god of the love-god.
links.teaches: The poem moves from a lover's praise of one woman to the poet's claim for the man among many, the height of pleasure just before the hero's renunciation.

links.note: The king is set above the love-god among women; Tirumantiram 203 says even those who hold knowledge are infatuated with women who bewilder and cannot change a mind once bewildered.
links.teaches: The epic's compliment to the king and the Saiva verse's warning describe one hold, and the reader learns the praise is also a statement of how firm that hold is.

gains.a: The praise of the king as the love-god's love-god gains a hint that those who hold such knowledge are no safer than the ignorant.
gains.b: The verse's general warning gains a named king, a court and a chapter just before his own turning away.

source_issues: 2649-2650: the speaker and the women are not named in the verses and the subjects are inferred; கந்தி in 2649 may be a word for a nun.
2665-2666: the verses' pronouns are hard to fix.
2668-2673: the metre changes to short lines; 2668 ends with என்பவே.
